I would change Ryan’s code from **SC to UA**, and record the circumstances in a factual note. He has said he was not ill, so SC is inaccurate. His sister does not live with him and is not among the relatives covered by the stated DEP definition. None of the other codes fits.

I would make clear in the note that Ryan reported an unexpected family emergency and called Gary at 05:40, before his shift. **UA is the code required by these rules, not a finding that he failed to notify his team leader.**

Before noon, I would email payroll, the HR Manager and Gary, flagging the consequence: this will be Ryan’s second UA during probation and will trigger a termination letter. I would ask whether an authorised person can intervene before the run and, if not, request an urgent review of the decision and any applicable employment rights.

I would not assume that the email prevents the letter: the HR Manager is away, Gary will not read email until after his shift, and no power to halt the process has been specified. If nobody intervenes, the letter will be generated and sent. I would also tell Ryan what has happened and that I have requested a review, without promising the outcome.

Leaving SC in place would avoid the immediate trigger, but it would knowingly submit a false sickness code and conceal the underlying problem.
